mcqs.question: Once your browser knows the server's IP address, why does the packet still need to pass through several independent routers rather than being sent directly?
options: Because IP addresses only encode the final destination, not a path — each router along the way makes its own hop-by-hop forwarding decision based on its own routing table
Because DNS only resolves the first hop's address, not the final one
Because TCP requires packets to visit at least three routers before a connection can open
Because routers batch packets from multiple users before forwarding them
mcqs.explanation: No single device holds the whole path in advance — routing is inherently distributed, with each router deciding the next hop independently based on its own table. DNS resolves the destination address only, not a route (ruling out the DNS-first-hop claim); TCP has no minimum-hop requirement (ruling out the three-router requirement); and batching isn't why hops exist (ruling out the packet-batching claim).

mcqs.question: Why must the TLS handshake happen after the TCP handshake completes, not before or in parallel?
options: TLS certificates are only valid once a TCP sequence number has been assigned
TLS is layered on top of an already-open, reliable TCP connection — there's no ordered, reliable byte stream to exchange ClientHello/ServerHello over until TCP has connected
Regulatory requirements mandate TCP complete first for auditing purposes
TLS uses the same three-way handshake packets as TCP, just re-labeled
mcqs.explanation: TLS assumes a reliable, ordered transport is already in place — it's built as a layer on top of TCP, not a replacement for it, so it needs TCP's handshake done first. The other options invent mechanisms (certificate-sequence binding, regulation, shared packets) that don't reflect how TLS actually works.

mcqs.question: A site loads slowly on every single visit, including repeat visits where the connection is already warm. Where should you look first?
options: DNS resolution time, since it's always the dominant cost
TCP and TLS handshake overhead, since those are the biggest cost on any request
The HTTP exchange itself or server-side processing, since connection setup costs are already eliminated on a warm/reused connection
The physical topology of the user's home network
mcqs.explanation: If slowness persists on reused connections, the setup-phase costs (DNS, TCP, TLS) are already paid and can't be the recurring bottleneck — the remaining suspect is the HTTP request/response itself or server processing time. DNS and handshake overhead (options 1 and 2) are exactly what a warm connection skips.
